We need count numbers <=1000 divisible by 3 or 5 but not by 15. Equivalent to numbers divisible by 3 or 5 minus those divisible by 15 (since divisible by both 3 and 5 is divisible by 15). So count = |A ∪ B| - |C|, where A: multiples of 3, B: multiples of 5, C: multiples of 15. Actually numbers divisible by 3 or 5 includes all that are in union; but we want exclude those divisible by 15. However note that numbers divisible by both 3 and 5 are exactly multiples of 15. So count = (#multiples of 3) + (#multiples of 5) - (#multiples of 15). Wait careful: Inclusion-exclusion gives |A∪B| = a+b-c. We want |(A∪B) \ C|, but since C is subset of A∩B (actually equal), we can compute |A∪B| - |C|. But |A∪B|=a+b-c. So result = a + b - c - c = a + b - 2c.

Compute: a = floor(1000/3) = 333. b = floor(1000/5)=200. c = floor(1000/15)=66. Then answer = 333+200-2*66=533-132=401? Wait compute: 333+200=533; 2c=132; 533-132=401.

Check: Another approach: Count multiples of 3 not multiple of 5 plus multiples of 5 not multiple of 3. Multiples of 3 not 5 = a - c = 333-66=267. Multiples of 5 not 3 = b - c =200-66=134. Sum =401. Good.

So answer: 401.
